name: CyBiasBench
description: CyBiasBench is a 630-session benchmark for measuring attack-selection bias in LLM agents performing authorized web-exploitation tasks. The release contains aggregate session records, per-family long-form records, and sanitized request-level HTTP traces for five agents across three intentionally vulnerable target applications. Metrics include selection rate, entropy H(X), most-selected family, Selection CR1, per-family ASR, session ASR, compliance, and requested-family ASR.
citeAs: @inproceedings{lim2026cybiasbench, title = {CyBiasBench: Benchmarking Bias in LLM Agents for Cyber-Attack Scenarios}, author = {Lim, Taein and Ju, Seongyong and Kim, Munhyeok and Kim, Hyunjun and Kim, Hoki}, booktitle = {NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track}, year = {2026}, url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07830} }
rai:dataLimitations: Scope is restricted to authorized web-exploitation tasks in isolated target environments.
The benchmark covers five agents, three target applications, four free-choice prompt conditions, and ten requested attack families for steering.
Measurements are HTTP-level; raw payload bodies, response bodies, headers, exact timestamps, and agent chain-of-thought are not released.
Per-family attempt counts are agent-driven in the bias observation setting, so rare families can have wider uncertainty.
The bias injection setting studies explicit single-family steering; softer steering regimes are not covered.
rai:dataBiases: The target applications emphasize web vulnerabilities and do not cover binary, kernel, hardware, cloud-native, or enterprise lateral-movement tasks.
The agent roster is a snapshot of five model families available at data collection time.
Success verification is rule-based and target-specific; false negatives are possible when an agent succeeds through an unintended path.
Selection metrics are less sensitive than success metrics to target difficulty, but still reflect the benchmark target and prompt distribution.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: No personal or user-generated content is included.
All sessions ran in isolated benchmark environments against intentionally vulnerable target applications with synthetic data.
The release removes raw bodies, headers, fine-grained timing, run identifiers, environment-specific identifiers, and provider credentials.
rai:dataUseCases: Quantifying attack-selection bias in LLM agents under matched target and prompt conditions.
Studying whether explicit requested-family steering changes allocation, compliance, and attack performance.
Reproducing the paper figures and tables from released aggregate and trace data.
Defensive and methodological research on behavioral auditing of tool-using agents.
Not for training, fine-tuning, or distilling agents to attack real-world systems.

rai:dataSocialImpact: CyBiasBench is intended to support defensive and measurement-oriented research by making LLM offensive-agent behavior quantifiable and comparable. Positive impacts include more rigorous bias audits of agentic security tooling and reproducible evaluation methodology. The main dual-use risk is that aggregate behavioral patterns could inform misuse; mitigations include releasing only sanitized traces and aggregates, withholding raw payload bodies and agent reasoning, using only intentionally vulnerable target applications, and documenting responsible-use restrictions.
rai:dataCollection: Data were collected from first-party benchmark runs between February 2026 and April 2026. Five LLM coding agents operated inside isolated Docker networks against intentionally vulnerable target applications under matched prompts, output formats, tools, and logging. HTTP traffic was captured through an intercepting proxy and LLM API usage through a LiteLLM proxy.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: No human annotation was used. Attack-vs-non-attack classification, attack-family labeling, CAPEC/CWE mapping, and success flags were produced by released rule-based classifiers and target-specific response heuristics.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Per-session HTTP traces and API logs were reduced to aggregate records, per-family long-form tables, and sanitized request-level traces. Sanitization removes raw request and response bodies, headers, exact timestamps, run identifiers, environment-specific identifiers, credentials, and verbatim agent reasoning while retaining request order, path, method, status code, labels, and short non-payload success evidence.
